claims.text: Periodic interfaces between adjacent HEA layers act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Periodic interfaces impede dislocation climb.
A multilayer HEA coating has less creep than a composition- and thickness-equivalent monolithic HEA coating.
The individual HEA layers have BCC or FCC structures.
Significant lattice distortion is typical of HEAs.
Engineered interfaces interrupt continuous dislocation channels.
Engineered interfaces encourage strain partitioning between layers.
High lattice distortion in HEAs retards dislocation motion.
Coherent or semi-coherent multilayer interfaces force dislocations to change direction or pile up.
Interruption of dislocation paths reduces continuous dislocation climb and glide.
Suppression of continuous dislocation climb and glide lowers the creep strain rate.
Multilayer HEA coatings will have lower steady-state creep rates than monolithic HEA coatings.
Multilayer HEA coatings will retain more yield strength under creep conditions than monolithic HEA coatings.
Creep deformation in HEAs can be active at moderate to high temperatures under sustained stress.
The proposed interface-barrier effect applies when individual layer thicknesses are on the order of tens to hundreds of nanometers.
Interdiffusion at extreme service conditions may weaken the beneficial interface-barrier effect.
Oxidation at extreme service conditions may weaken the beneficial interface-barrier effect.
The roles of interface chemistry, interface coherence, and long-term interdiffusion are not fully established.
The effects of layer-thickness variation and minor interfacial composition fluctuations on barrier efficiency are uncertain.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant creep-rate reduction and greater yield-strength retention, together with interfacial dislocation pile-ups, would falsify the hypothesis.
